newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: New Congo plans $300 mln revamp of Shaba railway.
newsitem.headline: New Congo plans $300 mln revamp of Shaba railway.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of Congo plans to spend $300 million upgrading its rail link with South Africa.

Kasongo Tshikomba, director of former Zaire's railways, told Reuters the country would consider selling stakes in the railway, recently nationalised again, to foreign companies if the refurbishment succeeded.

The Belgian-South African Sizarail consortium took over in 1995 to get Zaire's rusting, state-operated transport system moving again. Roads in the country are appalling and air freight too expensive for bulk mineral exports.

Sizarail restored reliable traffic linking Lubumbashi, capital of mineral-rich Shaba province, to Zambia and on to South Africa, as well as upcountry to the riverboat port of Ilebo, where barges could ferry goods on down the Congo to Kinshasa. It also operated a line from Kamina to Kalemie, an inland port on Lake Tanganyika in eastern Zaire.

Shortly after ousting former president Mobutu Sese Seko last month, rebel leader Laurent Kabila's new government seized control of the railway, upsetting South African transport companies which operate trains or coaches along it.

Visiting European and U.S. analysts said Congo nationalised the railway about six weeks ago and that mining operations in the mineral-rich southern Shaba province were threatened because South Africa could halt the shipment of fuel needed to run transport.

"They refuse to send their trucks and trains in there unless they have some control over them. I've heard that some operations have shut down because there is no fuel," said Philippe Platteau, a businessman based in Kinshasa.
But Tshikomba said the Kabila government was willing to cooperate with the South Africans.
"We will control all the railways but will co-operate and deal with the South African railways for the exportation of cargo. We can't do it another way," Tshikomba said.
"Taking into account all the mining projects in (former Zaire), we have planned an investment project from 1997 to 1999 to refurbish the railroad," he said.
He said the upgrades would cost at least $300 million but declined to specify where the funding would come from.
"Three hundred million is the minimum needed just to refurbish everything to working order," Tshikomba said.

The new government has recognised that much of former Zaire's economic future rests with the profitable exploitation of minerals -- it is rich in copper and cobalt, among others -- and will try to facilitate this, analysts said.
"It's logical to want to utilise the resources in the ground but this is going to take time and investment," said William Coogan, managing director of Rothschilds Inc.
Analysts said they were unaware of where the new Congo planned to raise $300 million.
"It's a million here, a few million there. It'll take quite a while to gather," Coogan said.
Tshikomba said the government was considering expanding the rail line to the north of the country.
"Very soon we will have a plan which is being studied and under discussion right now for expansion as well, but it's more a refurbishing beyond what we are talking about," he said.
He also said the government might consider part-privatising the railroad in the future.
"It's under review to sell stakes but it all depends on how competently this $300 million can be spent."
